newsitem.title: CHINA: Emotions overflow at farewell for China's Deng.
newsitem.headline: Emotions overflow at farewell for China's Deng.

text.p: China cremated paramount leader Deng Xiaoping on Monday after his successor President Jiang Zemin and the elite of the ruling Communist Party bowed before the body of the man who transformed the nation.
China's millions saw an extensive televised view of their deceased leader lying in a grey Mao suit, a red Communist Party flag draped on his body and surrounded by a mass of flowers.
One of his three daughters, Deng Nan, embraced and kissed her father, state television showed. Another daughter, Deng Rong, cried out: "You are not dead."
In front of Deng's remains was a huge floral arrangement presented by his wife, Zhuo Lin, and their children, with a silk streamer carrying the words: "We will love you forever."
"Eternal Glory to Comrade Deng Xiaoping," read a banner above his body in the 301 military hospital where his body had lain since he died last Wednesday, aged 92.

His designated heir Jiang, Premier Li Peng, the five other members of the all-powerful Politburo and other leaders, wearing black armbands and with white paper flowers of mourning in their buttonholes, bowed three times before the body.

A white van bedecked with black and yellow ribbons, the colours of mourning, carried Deng's body at a stately pace from the hospital to Babaoshan cemetery in western Beijing where Chinese communism's heroes are traditionally laid to rest.
"Scatter Hot Tears for Comrade Xiaoping," read a banner with black characters held up by one group of people.
"Go gently, Xiaoping," read another.

Hundreds of armed police, a fraction of the huge security force activated as China treads warily along the road of political transition, lined streets along the 2.5-km (1.5-mile) route to the cemetery.

The cortege moved at a pace allowing a crowd officially estimated at 100,000 lining the route a last glimpse of the man who ruled China for 18 years with a blend of capitalist-style economic policies and ruthless political control.
As the cavalcade passed, people stood on roofs of buildings or climbed up lamp posts for a better view.

But some residents did not know Deng's body was to be moved and were upset that their routine had been disrupted. "Hey, move it, some of us have to go to work," grumbled one middle-aged woman pushing her bicycle through the crowd.
After the cremation, the ashes were to be taken to the cavernous Great Hall of the People on Tiananmen Square where 10,000 people are due to attend a memorial service on Tuesday.
Deng, an opponent of the leadership cult around his predecessor Mao Zedong, made clear he wanted more restrained mourning than the near-hysteria that followed Mao's demise in 1976.
No foreign dignitaries have been invited to witness Tuesday's rites in the Great Hall. Deng's ashes will be scattered at sea.
Deng's family requested that his body not be put on display, that his corneas be donated to an eye bank and his body offered for medical dissection before cremation.
Medical officials said on Monday that the corneas had gone to China's premier eye hospital.
"Our whole hospital is very moved by this," said a nurse at the Tongren hospital in Beijing, the capital's only eye bank.
"We hope they will provide hope and light for our future," she said. It was not known whether the corneas would in fact be used.

Since Deng's death, authorities have heightened their security watch around the capital and especially in Tiananmen Square, the vast central space where, in 1989, student-led protests were crushed by troops and tanks at Deng's behest.
